transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, really appreciate you taking the time. quick intro — I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood Inference. today daniel will walk through the SDK quickstart and environment setup.
[00:09] Maya: thanks Sofia, excited — we want to get devs unblocked this week. Liam's here to understand constraints.
[00:15] Daniel: cool, quick agenda: 1) auth patterns 2) python/ts quickstart 3) env & CI secret patterns 4) Console + Optimize hints, and 5) Q&A and next steps.
[00:28] Priya: we are especially interested in private deployments and VPC peering — also how you rotate keys in CI.
[00:35] Daniel: noted. starting with auth: Redwood supports API keys for hosted, dedicated tokens for Reserved, and Private with customer-managed KMS + ephemeral certs for on-prem, so you can do SAML SSO plus RBAC. small caveat: when using ephemeral creds with our private control plane, you'll need to open a couple of egress endpoints — we'll send the network diagram.
[00:55] Daniel: demo time — Python quickstart. pip install redwood-sdk (note: the package name in the demo might show as redwood-infer on the pip index, we sometimes see aliases). code snippet:
    from redwood import RedwoodClient
    client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
    resp = client.generate('Summarize the last quarter customer feedback')
I know that the repo we share uses async calls and streaming examples.
[01:25] Maya: is there a difference in behavior if we call the hosted API vs dedicated? we want predictable p99 latency.
[01:33] Daniel: yes — hosted picks fastest regional pool, dedicated pins to your reserved nodes with better p99. you can also set routing policy in the request header to prefer low-latency nodes. note: batching heuristics are automatic but can be tuned per route.
[01:50] Alex: jumping in — for TypeScript the import is similar: npm install @redwood/inference, and you set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or use the SDK's credential provider for CI. our example repo has a github actions job showing secrets usage.
[02:08] Priya: okay about secrets — we use HashiCorp Vault in CI. can we inject ephemeral tokens into Github Actions?
[02:15] Daniel: yes, we support short-lived tokens via our token exchange API. flow is: Vault -> exchange for short-lived Redwood token -> set as env in action. we have a sample action script (we'll share). small transcription note: sometimes the docs reference token-exchange as token-exhange in older docs.
[02:37] Liam: on data residency: our legal wants logs retained for five years but only accessible to us. how do audit logs look?
[02:44] Sofia: Redwood Console offers per-tenant audit logs, exportable to S3, and with Private you can keep logs in your account and hook to your KMS. we'll attach the retention options and the export playbook.
[02:59] Maya: could you quickly show the Console route config?
[03:05] Daniel: yes — Console has per-route config for batching, kv cache TTLs, and quantization profile selection, but the UI name might show as "Model Profile" in some builds. here's a quick live snippet — (screen share) you set a route, pick model family, set batch window (ms) and max batch size. our default for low-latency is small batch / aggressive prefix cache.
[03:40] Daniel: now Optimize suggestions: for a median payload of 512 tokens, we typically recommend int8 quantized variants plus prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts. that drops cost ~30-50%. there's a tradeoff: aggressive quant can slightly alter output distribution — we recommend evals against your prompt set.
[04:05] Maya: we will need an eval harness, we use pytest and a small ml-eval lib. can you provide sample test harness?
[04:13] Alex: yes, sample harness in the repo; also we have a postman collection and a simple node script for load testing.
[04:20] Priya: for private — what's required network-wise?
[04:24] Daniel: for VPC private deployment you need to allow outbound to a set of control-plane IPs for management; data plane can be fully internal if using on-prem package. we'll send the list (again arguably sometimes shows as controlplane in docs).
[04:41] Noah: any gotchas around streaming responses in TS? we saw some choppy partials in an earlier demo.
[04:47] Alex: streaming uses SSE or websockets depending on SDK call; for Node we recommend the eventsource approach. choppy partials often due to small buffer windows in proxies — we recommend configuring keepalive and disabling chunked buffering in the corporate proxy.
[05:05] Liam: how about cost model? we want predictable unit economics for embeddings and chat.
[05:12] Sofia: hosted is per-token; dedicated gives committed throughput pricing plus lower per-token; Optimize helps by suggesting batching and cache to reduce tokens sent. we can apply usage caps per team in Console.
[05:28] Maya: any SSO integrations? we use Okta.
[05:31] Daniel: yes SSO via SAML, SCIM provisioning for accounts, and RBAC roles map to Console rights. older docs sometimes say OIDC but we primarily support SAML for enterprise customers.
[05:45] Priya: security: we need SOC2 report and a network diagram. also detail on KMS rotations.
[05:51] Sofia: we'll email SOC2, pen test summary, and a KMS rotation whitepaper. for Private you can bring your own KMS and have HSM-backed keys.
[06:05] Daniel: quick troubleshooting note: if SDK reports kv cache misses unexpectedly, ensure you pass stable cache-key across requests; sometimes clients generate ephemeral keys per request by accident.
[06:18] Maya: can you show the repo structure?
[06:21] Daniel: sure — repo has /python-quickstart, /ts-quickstart, /github-actions, /examples/streaming, /playbooks/optimize. our python example uses async and a helper that auto-retries 429s with exponential backoff. the package in the example uses REDWOOD_API_URL env var to point to sandbox.
[06:45] Maya: is sandbox usable for POC? we need isolation.
[06:48] Sofia: yes, we can spin up a sandbox org for Emberlane with isolated tokens and a dedicated small pool for the POC. data retention default is 30 days for sandboxes but we can configure.
[07:00] Noah: about model versions — how do rollouts work?
[07:03] Daniel: Console supports version pinning per route, canary rollouts and automatic fallback to prior version on error. the UI label might say rollout policy or traffic-split depending on build.
[07:20] Liam: rough timeline if we do POC? we want something by EOM.
[07:25] Sofia: we can do a 2-week POC: week 1 env & auth + quickstart + baseline latency runs; week 2 optimize and evals. we'll coordinate dates after you confirm peering window.
[07:40] Priya: firewall question — which ports?
[07:43] Daniel: HTTPS outbound 443, and if you use private control plane there are a couple of management IPs on 443 as well; if you opt for on-prem data plane there are internal ports for gRPC, we will provide exact list.
[07:58] Maya: any anti-patterns developers hit?
[08:01] Alex: sending full documents for every prompt (no prefix cache), not using KV caching for repeated context, and over-large batch windows that increase latency. we added playbook tips in the repo.
[08:15] Sofia: okay, let's recap next steps. we'll send: sandbox creds + repo, security pack, network diagram, and schedule POC kick-off.
[08:25] Maya: good. last quick Q: can we run a basic latency test from our VPC?
[08:29] Daniel: yes we'll provide a small bench script (python + k6) that hits the sandbox, and we'll coordinate a 15-min run during the POC to compare p50/p99.
[08:40] Liam: awesome. thanks all.
[08:42] Sofia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite.
[08:45] (call ends, some crosstalk)
[08:50] Daniel (after call): note to self, send the token-exchange sample action, and double-check the repo readme for the correct pip package name.
